metaTitle: Best Heated Airer UK 2026: 3 Picks and Running Costs
metaDescription: Lakeland Dry:Soon, Minky 4 Tier or Minky 12m? We compare drying space, load and timers, and work out the cost per hour at the 26.32p Ofgem price cap.
h1: Best heated airer UK 2026: which one to buy, and what it costs to run
answer: For most UK homes, the Lakeland Dry:Soon Deluxe 3-Tier is the heated airer to buy: 21 m of drying space, a 15 kg load, a built-in timer and a 300 W rating, about 7.9p an hour at the Ofgem cap of 26.32p/kWh (1 October to 31 December 2026). Want more room and a cover in the box? Minky’s 4 Tier. Smaller loads on a tighter budget? Minky’s 12m winged airer.

picks.why: It pairs a two-load capacity (21 m, 15 kg) with what matters day to day: an eye-level control panel, a built-in timer and an 8 cm folded depth. It is also the model independent testers keep naming, from The Telegraph (March 2026) to The Guardian (October 2026).
picks.bestFor: Families without a tumble dryer who dry a load most days and want the airer to switch itself off.

specs.Timer: built in, 1 to 12 hours; can also delay switch-on by up to 12 hours (instruction booklet)
specs.Guarantee: 3 years, as shown on Lakeland’s product page (1 November 2026)
specs.Running cost at 26.32p/kWh: about 7.9p an hour at the rated 300 W

picks.model: Minky 4 Tier sureDRI Heated 23m Clothes Airer with Cover (IH89294101)
picks.why: At 23 m and 20 kg it has the largest stated capacity in this guide, a cover comes in the box and the timer runs for up to 9 hours. The trade-offs: the top layer is not heated (Which? measured 20.3 m of heated rail), it folds to 15.5 cm, almost twice the Lakeland’s depth, and Minky gives a 1-year guarantee.
picks.bestFor: Large households, or anyone who wants a cover without buying it separately.

specs.Maximum load: 20 kg (3 kg per arm, 6 kg per layer, 2 kg on the top layer)
specs.Running cost at 26.32p/kWh: about 7.9p an hour at the rated 300 W

picks.why: A winged airer with 12 m of drying space on 19 rails and a 16 kg load limit that is cheaper to buy than our two tower picks. Minky quotes 8p an hour but gives no wattage. Expect slower drying than a tower: in Which?’s tests, winged airers took longer on average.
picks.bestFor: One- or two-person households drying small loads, and flats where a 1.3 m tower would be in the way.

specs.Running cost: 8p an hour (Minky’s figure; minky.com gives no wattage or unit rate)

criteria.name: Drying space and load
criteria.explanation: Metres of heated rail and kilograms of wet washing, as the maker states them. A 21 m tower takes roughly two machine loads; a 12 m winged airer about one. This decides whether you dry a wash in one go or in two sessions.

criteria.name: Running cost
criteria.explanation: Rated wattage multiplied by the Ofgem unit rate (26.32p/kWh, 1 October to 31 December 2026). We don’t score pence-per-hour claims that hide the wattage or the unit rate behind them, so a model with no published wattage scores lower here.

criteria.name: Timer, controls and cover
criteria.explanation: A built-in timer lets the airer switch itself off, which matters because Lakeland advises against leaving any appliance running unattended overnight. Makers and The Telegraph say a made-to-fit cover speeds drying, but Which? found covered airers dried no faster in its tests, so the cover counts for less than the timer.

criteria.name: Independent test results
criteria.explanation: Published findings from Which?, The Telegraph and The Guardian, quoted with their dates. We do not test products ourselves.

criteria.name: Storage
criteria.explanation: Folded depth and weight. At 8 cm an airer slides behind a door or down the side of a wardrobe; at 15.5 cm it needs a cupboard.

criteria.name: Guarantee and UK support
criteria.explanation: Length of guarantee stated by the maker or seller, and whether there is a UK customer-care team.

sections.h2: What a heated airer costs to run at today’s price cap
sections.html:
Ofgem’s price cap for 1 October to 31 December 2026 sets an average electricity unit rate of 26.32p per kWh for Direct Debit customers on a standard variable tariff in England, Scotland and Wales (announced 26 August 2026). That rate already reflects the government’s removal of VAT from electricity bills from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, so there is nothing to add on top. The standing charge of 54.83p a day is paid whether the airer is on or not, so we leave it out.

The sum is simple: watts ÷ 1,000 × hours × unit rate.

  • 198 W (Dry:Soon Mini): about 5.2p an hour, or 31p for a 6-hour session.
  • 300 W (Dry:Soon Deluxe and Standard, Minky 3 and 4 Tier, Beldray 3 Tier): about 7.9p an hour, 47p for 6 hours, and 95p if you run a Deluxe for its full 12-hour timer.
  • Three 6-hour sessions a week on a 300 W airer: 156 sessions a year, about £74 if the rate stayed at 26.32p all year.

These figures assume the rated wattage for every hour, and real use can differ either way. The Telegraph metered the Dry:Soon Deluxe at 0.331 kWh in an hour, about 8.7p at today’s cap. Lakeland says its Standard and Mini Dry:Soon airers have thermostatic control, and Which?, which measures real consumption, found the models it tested cost from as little as 4p to about 29p an hour (at its own rate of 24.67p/kWh).

Ofgem announces the next cap on 25 November 2026, for 1 January to 31 March 2027, and we will recalculate these figures then. In Northern Ireland, or on a fixed or time-of-use tariff, use the unit rate on your own bill.

sections.h2: Why the “pence per hour” on the box never matches
sections.html:
Every maker prints a running cost, but each works it out at a different unit rate, and not all of them say which. Lakeland’s Deluxe page says 8p an hour, worked out at 26.11p/kWh (July 2026); Minky’s 12m page also says 8p, with no rate attached. Dunelm calculates at 26p/kWh on its 3 Tier listing; Which? uses 24.67p/kWh. A figure written when electricity cost more will look worse than it is today, and one written at a lower rate will flatter the airer.

The wattage is the number to compare. If a listing gives a cost per hour but no wattage, as Minky’s own 12m page does, ask the seller or check the rating plate before you buy.

We scored each model on our six weighted criteria. The order follows the scores, not price or clicks.

  • Lakeland Dry:Soon Deluxe leads on the criteria that carry the most weight together: two-load capacity, a built-in timer that can also delay the start, the slimmest folded depth (8 cm), the longest guarantee shown (3 years on Lakeland’s page) and the strongest run of independent picks.
  • Minky 4 Tier sureDRI beats it on stated space (23 m, 20 kg) and includes the cover, but Which? measured only 20.3 m of that as heated, it folds to 15.5 cm, has a 1-year guarantee and has not been named a winner by the testers we cite.
  • Minky 12m winged takes the budget slot. Price is not one of our weighted criteria, so this slot goes to a cheaper model that still covers the basics: 12 m of rail and a 16 kg load limit from a maker with a UK customer-care team. On the weights it scores below the towers on space, drying speed and running cost, which we can’t calculate because Minky gives no wattage. If your budget stretches further, the Beldray 3 Tier (300 W, 20 m, folds to 8 cm) scores higher on our criteria, although it has no timer.

sections.h2: Lakeland Dry:Soon Deluxe 3-Tier: the one testers keep picking
sections.html:
Lakeland has sold Dry:Soon heated airers since 2008, and the Deluxe is the top of the tower range. It shares the Standard model’s 21 m and 15 kg, but adds an eye-level control panel, easier front loading and a timer. Lakeland’s instructions say you can set it to switch off, or to come on, up to 12 hours ahead.

The folding shelves are the practical win: open them all for a full load, lay knitwear flat on a shelf, or open only the top tier to hang a sheet without it touching the floor. Folded, it is 8 cm deep. Castors and the fitted cover are extras; Lakeland sells the cover as a bundle, and that bundle is the version The Guardian named best overall in its 26 October 2026 update.

Limits: it is a large frame at 70 × 74 × 132.5 cm when open, and the cover is not in the box unless you buy the bundle.

sections.h2: Minky 4 Tier sureDRI 23m: the most room, with the cover included
sections.html:
Minky, a Rochdale firm with a UK customer-care team, makes the largest tower in this guide. Its angled “Vertex” arms hold garments apart so air can move between them, and the top layer adds space for socks and smalls, although its rungs are not heated: The Telegraph found the top tier doesn’t warm up, and Which? measured 20.3 m of heated rail out of 22.9 m. The 300 W rating is the same as the Lakeland’s, so the cost per hour is the same, about 7.9p at the current cap.

The cover comes in the box, and the timer can be set for up to 9 hours. Minky lists a weight capacity per arm (3 kg) and per layer (6 kg), which is worth respecting: spread heavy towels across the tiers rather than piling them on one.

Limits: it folds to 15.5 cm, almost twice the Dry:Soon’s depth, weighs 5.1 kg and comes with a 1-year guarantee. If you don’t need the cover or the extra tier, the Minky 3 Tier sureDRI 21m (300 W, 18 kg) is the same design without them.

sections.h2: Minky Heated 12m winged: the budget pick for smaller loads
sections.html:
Winged airers are the classic clothes horse with heated bars: a central section and two fold-out wings. Minky’s 12m model has 19 rails, takes up to 16 kg and folds away between uses. Minky quotes 8p an hour to run, although its own page does not give the wattage.

Which?’s analysis (first published in November 2023, updated in March 2026) found winged airers a little cheaper to run than towers on average (6p against 8p an hour) but noticeably slower, at around 5 hours 54 minutes for a small cotton load against 4 hours 40 minutes for towers. That suits someone drying a few items most days rather than a family wash.

Limits: less space than any tower here, long items need the wings, and a cover is an extra.

sections.h2: Tower, winged, pod or cabinet: which shape suits you
sections.html:
• Tower (3 or 4 tiers): the most drying space for the floor area, warmer bars and the best balance of speed and cost in Which?’s analysis. Best for families.
  • Winged: low, light and cheaper to buy; slower, and better for small loads.
  • Drying pod: a fan heater blows warm air through a zipped enclosure holding garments on hangers. Which? found pods dried a small cotton load in about 2 hours 13 minutes on average, but cost more per load because they hold less (57p against 35p for heated airers, at 24.67p/kWh).
  • Drying cabinet: Lakeland’s Dry:Soon cabinet is rated at 1,200 W, about 31.6p an hour at 26.32p/kWh. It is a tumble-dryer substitute in cost terms, not a cheap airer.

sections.h2: Heated airer, tumble dryer or dehumidifier?
sections.html:
Which?’s current guide (page last checked October 2026) puts numbers on it. Drying three small (2.15 kg) cotton loads a week costs just over £46 a year on a heated airer, against around £79 for a condenser and £93 for a vented tumble dryer. For three large loads a week the order flips: about £112 a year on a heated airer, because you need several sessions per load, against around £58 for the average tumble dryer. If you already own a heat-pump tumble dryer, Which? says to stick with it.

A heated airer does not remove the water from your clothes, it moves it into the room. Which? warns that this raises the risk of condensation and suggests opening a window or running a dehumidifier, which it says also helps clothes dry faster. Many dehumidifiers sold in the UK have a laundry mode for exactly this.

sections.h2: Where to buy a heated airer in the UK
sections.html:
• Lakeland sells Dry:Soon direct, including the airer-and-cover bundles, and also through Amazon. Check the guarantee where you buy: Lakeland’s own product page shows a 3-year guarantee.
  • Minky sells direct from Rochdale and through retailers including Argos, Dunelm and Currys, as well as Amazon. Retailer listings of the same airer sometimes use a different model code, so check the drying space and load limit against minky.com.
  • Dunelm and Argos sell own-brand heated airers alongside Minky. The Telegraph named Dunelm’s 3 Tier Heated Airer its best value pick in March 2026.
  • Lidl and Aldi sell heated airers from time to time as limited-time offers. Compare wattage, drying space, load limit and guarantee with the models above before you buy.

• Don’t leave it running unattended overnight. That is Lakeland’s advice; set a built-in timer instead.
  • Skip the smart plug. The Dry:Soon Deluxe instructions we read say not to connect it to an external timer or remote-control system.
  • Unfold fully before loading and switching on, and load evenly: the Deluxe’s limit is 15 kg, and an unbalanced load can tip it.
  • Use the cover made for your model, not a blanket or a duvet. Lakeland’s instructions for its heated winged airer, for example, say not to cover it with a duvet or thick blanket, to avoid overheating.
  • Turn and move the washing. Which? notes that airers dry best where fabric touches the bars, and its drying times assume the laundry is rotated.
  • Ventilate or dehumidify the room, especially in winter, to keep condensation and mould off windows and walls.

faq.q: Are heated clothes airers any good?
faq.a: Yes, for small and medium loads. Which? found the heated airers it tested typically took four to seven hours to dry a small (2.15 kg) cotton load: much faster than an unheated airer, but slower than a tumble dryer. In its tests, tower airers such as the Lakeland Dry:Soon Deluxe dried faster on average than winged models.

faq.q: How much does a heated airer cost to run per hour?
faq.a: Multiply the wattage by the unit rate. At the Ofgem cap of 26.32p/kWh (1 October to 31 December 2026), a 300 W airer costs about 7.9p an hour and a 198 W airer about 5.2p, at full power. Most airers in this guide are rated between about 200 and 300 W.

faq.q: Is a heated airer cheaper than a tumble dryer?
faq.a: For small loads, yes. Which? puts three small loads a week at just over £46 a year on a heated airer, against around £79 for a condenser dryer. For three large loads a week a tumble dryer is cheaper (about £58 against £112), and Which? puts a heat-pump dryer at around £46 a year for those large loads.

faq.q: Can you leave a heated airer on overnight?
faq.a: Lakeland advises against leaving any electrical appliance running unattended overnight. If you dry in the evening, choose a model with a built-in timer, such as the Dry:Soon Deluxe (up to 12 hours) or the Minky 4 Tier sureDRI (up to 9 hours), so it switches itself off.

faq.q: Do I need a heated airer cover?
faq.a: It isn’t essential, and testers disagree. Lakeland and Minky say a fitted cover traps heat and speeds drying, and The Guardian’s best overall pick is the Dry:Soon Deluxe sold with its cover. Which? found the three covered airers it tested dried no faster than those without, which it puts down to humid air trapped under the cover. If you buy one, choose the vented cover made for your model, never a blanket.

faq.q: Can I use a smart plug with a heated airer?
faq.a: Check the instructions first. The Dry:Soon Deluxe instructions we read say not to connect it to an external timer or remote-control system, which rules out a smart plug. Use the built-in timer instead.

faq.q: Does Russell Hobbs make a heated airer?
faq.a: The Russell Hobbs airers we found at UK retailers on 1 November 2026, such as the 3-tier LA073785EU7 (15 m of drying space), are unheated. Make sure a listing says “heated” and gives a wattage before you buy.

faq.q: Heated airer or dehumidifier for drying clothes indoors?
faq.a: They do different jobs. A heated airer warms the clothes; a dehumidifier pulls the moisture they release out of the air. In a cold, damp home it makes sense to use both: dry on the airer and run the dehumidifier in the same room with the door shut.

faq.q: Will heated airer running costs change in January?
faq.a: Possibly. Ofgem announces the next price cap on 25 November 2026, for 1 January to 31 March 2027. We will recalculate the pence-per-hour figures on this page when it does.

independentTesters.name: Which?
independentTesters.note: Best heated clothes airers (page last checked October 2026; test dates July 2023, December 2023, September 2024 and October 2025): more than 25 heated airers and drying pods tested for drying speed, running cost, stability and capacity. Running costs at 24.67p/kWh: the best cost as little as 4p an hour, the most expensive around 29p. Airers typically took four to seven hours to dry a 2.15 kg cotton load. The Dry:Soon Deluxe was last tested in September 2024. Scores and recommendations are for members only.

independentTesters.name: Which?
independentTesters.note: Are heated airers worth it? (first published 3 November 2023, updated 27 March 2026): tower airers averaged 4 hours 40 minutes for a small cotton load at about 8p an hour; winged airers averaged 5 hours 54 minutes at about 6p; drying pods averaged 2 hours 13 minutes but cost more per load. The three airers tested with covers dried no faster than those without. Running costs at 24.67p/kWh.

independentTesters.name: The Telegraph
independentTesters.note: The best heated clothes airers (Flora Baker, published 19 March 2026): Best Buy, Lakeland Dry:Soon Deluxe 3-Tier; Best Value, Dunelm 3 Tier Heated Airer; best winged, Minky SureDri 15m XL with cover. The airers tested cost 7p to 28p an hour, measured with a smart plug.

independentTesters.name: The Guardian (The Filter)
independentTesters.note: The best heated clothes airers (Jane Hoskyn, first published 18 October 2024, updated 26 October 2026): 19 airers tested over two years, with half-hourly weigh-ins of identical small (4 kg) and large (8 kg) loads. Best overall: Lakeland Dry:Soon Deluxe 3-tier heated airer and cover; best budget: Black+Decker heated winged airer; best for fast drying: Minky SureDri Heat Pod Pro.
